extracted.intended_audience: readers of travel/natural-history prose and writers studying descriptive/observational narrative techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Writing and presenting first-person travel / natural-history observations: describing materials, peoples, practices, and empirical field results, and drawing inferences from those observations. Uses anecdote, enumeration, functional explanation, and simple empirical tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not draw general conclusions from a very partial view of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: “From this we may learn two things: first, not to draw general conclusions from a very partial view of nature; and secondly, that trees and fruits, no less than the varied productions of the animal kingdom, do not appear to be organized with exclusive reference to the use and convenience of man.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit admonition against overgeneralization and anthropocentric inference. Use sufficiently broad observation before extrapolating general laws; flag when conclusions are based on limited data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid assuming nature is organized solely for human convenience
rubrics_metrics.description: “...that trees and fruits, no less than the varied productions of the animal kingdom, do not appear to be organized with exclusive reference to the use and convenience of man.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting natural features, resist interpreting form/purpose only in human terms. Present multiple possible functions or independent explanations rather than anthropomorphic teleology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrate utility by enumerating material qualities and uses (example: Bamboo)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Their strength, lightness, smoothness, straightness, roundness and hollowness, the facility and regularity with which they can be split, their many different sizes, the varying length of their joints, the ease with which they can be cut and with which holes can be made through them, their hardness outside, their freedom from any pronounced taste or smell, their great abundance, and the rapidity of their growth and increase, are all qualities which render them useful for a hundred different purposes...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List concrete, sensory and mechanical qualities of a material and follow with specific examples of applications and comparisons to alternatives (labor saved, performance differences). Use enumeration to build a persuasive case for utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small quotidian details as evidence for larger cultural/character inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: “Even these apparently trifling matters may assist us to form a truer estimate of the Dyaks' character and social condition. We learn thereby, that these people have passed beyond that first stage of savage life ...” (example: the cat's-cradle anecdote)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and present ordinary, everyday behaviors or amusements and show how they support inferences about social organization, mental capacity, or civilization. Small, concrete anecdotes can act as evidence in place of abstract claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain designs and practices by function and available resources (bridges, ladders, steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed description of Dyak bridges and steps: construction from crossing bamboos, suspension from overhanging trees, use of diagonal struts to avoid placing posts in streams, pegged bamboo steps for slippery ground, rapid replacement of decaying materials because of local abundance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing technology or built form, show how material properties and environmental constraints determine design. Explain both construction details and the practical reasoning (economy, safety, maintenance) behind them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support observational claims with empirical data and contextual conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The nightly moth-collection table giving Date, No. of Moths, and Remarks (weather conditions), and the summary discussion linking high counts to 'very wet and dark nights'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include quantitative records (dates, counts, conditions) when asserting patterns. Pair numerical data with contextual notes (weather, location, setup) and use the data to test or illustrate hypotheses about causal conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give concrete, actionable field recommendations based on experience
rubrics_metrics.description: “I feel sure that ... it would well repay them to carry a small framed verandah, or a verandah-shaped tent of white canvas, to set up in every favourable situation, as a means of making a collection of nocturnal Lepidoptera ... I make the suggestion here, because no one would suspect the enormous difference in results that such an apparatus would produce...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When advising practitioners, specify exact equipment or procedures, explain why they matter (observed efficacy), and note the surprising or counterintuitive benefits—don’t remain vague.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argumentative method: enumerate known hypotheses then evaluate against observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of Malthus's listed checks to population (starvation, disease, war, infanticide, immorality, infertility) followed by the author's evaluation that infertility (or reduced births due to women's hard labour) best fits the Dyak data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lay out competing theories or causes explicitly, examine available observational evidence for each, and justify selection of the most plausible explanation. Make the reasoning chain clear from premises to conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparison and historical contrast to evaluate governance and social change
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast of life under previous Malay tyranny with Sir James Brooke's administration: protection from slaving and robbery, restoration of property rights, and the population's resulting gratitude and mythologizing of Brooke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing institutions or social change, juxtapose prior and current states, provide concrete consequences and examples, and include local perceptions or reactions to illustrate effects.
